opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think a big part of it is that language is the interface humans already use for almost everything. When a model can read and write text well, it can immediately plug into a huge range of tasks like answering questions, writing code, summarizing documents, and reasoning through problems. You don't need to build a separate system for each one. The output is something people can use directly.

Vision has been very successful, but historically it was more of a component. You'd train a detector or a segmentation model, and it became one piece inside a larger pipeline, say in a self-driving stack or a medical imaging tool. That's valuable, but the average person never talks to an ImageNet classifier. With language models, the model itself became the product, and everyone could try it.

There's also a data and objective story. Text on the internet is already highly compressed and semantic. Humans have done a lot of the abstraction work by choosing words. So next-token prediction on text forces the model to learn knowledge, logic, and some world modeling fairly directly. Pixels are much more redundant and low-level. Predicting the next pixel, or reconstructing masked patches, doesn't obviously push the model toward the high-level understanding we care about, at least not as efficiently. We've had good self-supervised methods in vision, but we haven't found an objective as simple and scalable as next-token prediction that gives you general capability.

And language gives you a natural task specification. You can just tell the model what you want. In vision, defining the task usually meant choosing labels and datasets ahead of time. Once the model could take instructions in language, it became general-purpose.

So it's not that vision was failing. Language turned out to be the right medium for generality, both for training signal and for how humans interact with the system. Now the interesting question is how vision fits into that, whether it stays a perception module feeding language models, or whether we eventually find a way for visual learning to scale with the same kind of generality.

r001.rationale: The response says pixels are redundant and low-level, but does not attribute the difficulty to visual data bandwidth exceeding available compute.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss multimodal language models revisiting image regions after encoding.

r003.rationale: It discusses limitations of visual learning objectives, but does not identify the vision encoder as a bottleneck that the language model cannot fix.

r004.rationale: It says humans add abstraction by choosing words, but does not characterize language as a conceptual representation of nature already learned by humans and supplied to language models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, that's a question I think about a lot, because I spent most of my career in vision, and in some sense vision was "solved" to a surprising degree long before language got there. We had ImageNet classifiers beating humans around 2015. We had detection, segmentation, all of that working pretty well. And yet none of that produced the kind of societal moment that ChatGPT did.

I think there are a few reasons, and they're kind of layered.

The first is just the interface. Language is the native interface for humans to express what they want. If I give you an image classifier, you have to figure out what to do with a thousand class labels. If I give you a language model, you just type what you want and it does something. The output is also something you can immediately use. A paragraph is a deliverable. A bounding box is not. So the gap between "the model works" and "a normal person gets value out of it" was enormous for vision and almost zero for language.

The second is that language is a much more general substrate. When you train on text, you're not just learning a perception task, you're learning a compressed version of a huge amount of human knowledge and reasoning, because people wrote all of that down. Images don't come with that. An image of a cat tells you what a cat looks like, but it doesn't tell you why cats are mammals or how to write a contract. So the same architecture, the same training recipe, ends up covering coding, writing, question answering, translation, all at once. In vision we had to build a separate model for almost every task, and that fragmentation really limited how far any one model could spread.

Third, and this one I think is underappreciated, is that the pretraining objective in language is almost perfectly aligned with the downstream use. Next-token prediction is the task. You train on it, and then you use the model by having it predict tokens. In vision, we spent years on self-supervised objectives, contrastive learning, masked image modeling, and they were always a kind of proxy. You learn representations and then you have to fine-tune or attach a head to do anything useful. That extra step is where a lot of the generality leaks out.

And then the last thing is honestly just scale and data. The internet is mostly text, and text is cheap to store and easy to tokenize. The community discovered the scaling laws in language first, and once people saw that the curve kept going, the money followed. Vision had been somewhat stuck at ImageNet scale, a million images, for a long time partly because nobody was convinced that going to a billion would change anything qualitatively.

So I'd say vision was earlier, but it was earlier at a narrower thing. Language was later, but when it arrived, it arrived as a general-purpose tool with a human-friendly interface. I actually think vision is now going to benefit from this, because the lesson that a single model trained on a simple objective at huge scale can be general is going to be applied back to images and video. We're just a few years behind.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the availability and scale of text data, but does not say visual data exceeds the compute available to exploit it.

r002.rationale: It does not describe multimodal models revisiting image regions after encoding them into vision tokens.

r003.rationale: It does not identify the vision encoder as a bottleneck or say the language model cannot repair its representational shortcomings.

r004.rationale: The response says text contains human knowledge and reasoning, but does not characterize language as a conceptual representation of nature already learned by humans and supplied to language models.

astra-6.text:
I think a big part of it is that language is a very general interface. In computer vision, we made a lot of progress, but often we were working on a specific task: classify this image, detect objects, or segment an image. Those capabilities are useful, but you usually need to build a specialized system around them before people can use them.

With language models, you can describe what you want in natural language. The same model can help you write something, answer a question, or write code. That makes the capability much more accessible, including to people who don’t know anything about machine learning.

Language is also a medium in which people encode knowledge and describe how to solve problems. So learning to predict language can lead to capabilities that extend beyond what we might think of as a narrow language task. And once you put that into a conversational interface, people can explore those capabilities themselves. I think that combination—generality and ease of use—helps explain both the jump in capabilities and the speed of adoption.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses vision tasks being specialized, but does not attribute difficulty exploiting visual data to its bandwidth exceeding available compute.

r002.rationale: It says nothing about multimodal models revisiting image regions or image tokens.

r003.rationale: It does not identify a vision encoder as a bottleneck or discuss limits on what the language model can recover.

r004.rationale: It describes language as a general interface and a medium for encoding knowledge, but does not characterize it as a conceptual representation of nature learned by humans and supplied to language models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is that language is a very general interface. In computer vision, we made a lot of progress, but the tasks were often fairly specific: classify an image, detect objects, or segment a scene. Those are useful capabilities, but you usually need to build a separate system around them for each application.

With a language model, you can describe what you want in ordinary language. The same model can help you write code, summarize a document, or work through a question. That makes it much easier for people to try it and discover something useful without being machine learning experts.

And language connects to so many kinds of knowledge. Predicting text sounds like a narrow objective, but doing it well across a broad range of data pushes the model to learn capabilities that transfer to many tasks. So you have both a broadly useful model and a very accessible way to interact with it. I think that combination explains a lot of the jump in adoption.
